title: World Bank projects STEG annual losses before subsidy of 3.4-3.7 billion TND without TEREG and 2.3-3.1 billion with TEREG in 2026-2028

rootCauses.cause: The World Bank PAD reports that tariff increases were not being considered by the Government at that stage because of social vulnerability and economic competitiveness concerns. Its 2025-2028 model assumes no tariff increase and projects continuing negative net results before subsidy; this is a scenario assumption, not evidence that no later tariff change occurred.

The PAD forecasts gas prices of US$10.3/MMBtu in 2025, US$8.6 in 2026, US$8.2 in 2027 and US$7.8 in 2028, and says imported gas is partly indexed to Brent. A separate press summary reports Brent at US$91.21/bbl through August 2026 against a US$63.3/bbl 2026 budget assumption. Those are different commodities and periods; the PAD does not model a high-price sensitivity, so the press comparison does not establish a revised STEG cost forecast.

STEG had a substantial stock of arrears and debt, and the PAD projects high end-2028 liabilities even with the programme. The PAD attributes the with-programme liabilities scenario to clearing part of past arrears and improving collection; the available cited evidence does not isolate arrears as the cause of the projected annual pre-subsidy losses.

sections.heading: Verification status
sections.content:
The modelled losses in PAD Table 5 and the parliamentary proposal were checked independently as separate measures. No budget figure is presented as an outturn or as STEG’s realised loss. The 2026 comparison and 2027 company split are explicitly secondary.

**Independent review, 21 November 2026:** pass after corrections. Originals checked: World Bank TEREG appraisal document, p. 18 Table 5 and paragraphs 46-47, p. 1 summary, p. 25 paragraph 76 (SRC-TG-105; every value in the indicators confirmed); ARP budget committee report on the 2027 draft budget, rendered pages PDF 51-52 (printed 50-51): 11,846 MD subsidy expenditure, Brent at USD 80, the 7,090 MD grant booked as hydrocarbon support and shared between STIR and STEG, the 600 MD performance measures, the 172 MD cost of a USD 1 rise in Brent, and no STEG or STIR amounts in that passage (SRC-TG-174); La Presse, 22 October 2026 (SRC-TG-167), Managers, 28 October 2025 (SRC-TG-166) and Mosaique FM, 31 October 2026 (SRC-TG-170) for the press figures. Correction: the 7,090 MD indicator was labelled "hydrocarbon and electricity subsidies"; the committee report labels it hydrocarbon support, so the name was changed. The reviewer could not read the Arabic text layer for the 7,090, 172 and non-itemisation points; they were confirmed on the rendered pages. Independent teammate sign-off is outstanding; reviewer and author share the TahaGHZ identity, so the record is not validated.

sections.heading: Problem
sections.content:
The World Bank's April 2025 appraisal of Tunisia's 2025-2028 TEREG programme models STEG's net result before subsidy and corporate tax under two scenarios. Without TEREG, it forecasts a result of TND -3,720m in 2026 and -3,395m in 2028; with TEREG, TND -3,086m and -2,288m respectively. These correspond to annual projected losses of about TND 3.4-3.7bn without the programme and TND 2.3-3.1bn with it during 2026-2028 (SRC-TG-105). The PAD's 2025 values (-5,103m and -4,691m) are forecasts; this finding does not assert a 2025 outturn. For 2025-2028, the PAD gives undiscounted sums of TND -15,803m without TEREG and -12,852m with it, and estimates subsidy need is TND 2,045m lower with the programme over the same period (SRC-TG-105). The model assumes no tariff increase and a declining gas-price path. Under the with-programme scenario, supplier liabilities plus short- and long-term debt are projected at TND 18.8bn at end-2028, while tariff cost recovery is projected to rise from 60% to 80% (SRC-TG-105).

The parliamentary budget report proposes TND 7,090m for hydrocarbon support in 2027 and TND 11,846m in total subsidies (SRC-TG-174, PDF pp. 51–52). Press sources attribute TND 3,676m of the proposed grant to STEG and TND 3,414m to STIR (SRC-TG-167). The committee confirms the two beneficiaries but does not itemise their amounts in that passage. Appropriations and the PAD’s projected utility losses measure different things.

sections.heading: Root causes
sections.content:
- **Tariff and cost recovery assumptions.** The World Bank PAD reports that the Government was not considering tariff increases at that stage, citing social vulnerability and economic competitiveness concerns. Its modeled scenarios assume no increase (SRC-TG-105; see FND-TG-161). This is dated policy context and a model assumption, not evidence about subsequent decisions.
- **Fuel cost exposure and uncertain gas-price path.** The PAD forecasts gas prices of US$10.3/MMBtu in 2025, US$8.6 in 2026, US$8.2 in 2027 and US$7.8 in 2028, and says imported gas is partly indexed to Brent (SRC-TG-105). A separate press summary of draft-budget documents reports Brent at US$91.21/bbl through August 2026 against a US$63.3/bbl assumption in the 2026 finance law (SRC-TG-170). These are different commodities and periods; they do not establish an updated STEG gas-cost projection or a lower bound for PAD losses. That sensitivity remains unmodeled in the cited PAD.
- **Legacy arrears and liabilities.** The PAD states that clearing part of past arrears and improving collection would help STEG repay overdue supplier obligations. It projects TND 18.8bn in supplier liabilities and short- and long-term debt at end-2028 with TEREG (SRC-TG-105). La Presse separately reports that the draft 2027 budget proposes settling about TND 500m in STEG arrears for 2017-2023 (SRC-TG-167). These facts document a legacy balance-sheet burden but do not isolate arrears as the cause of modeled annual pre-subsidy losses.
- In the with-programme case, the World Bank attributes improved tariff cost recovery to fuel-cost reduction, a higher renewable share in power generation, and programme measures (SRC-TG-105, para. 47); see also FND-TG-102.

sections.heading: Evidence
sections.content:
- PAD Table 5 and paragraphs 46-47 (SRC-TG-105, p. 18): annual scenario results, undiscounted 2025-2028 totals, subsidy-need reduction, liabilities, cost recovery, gas-price path and the no-tariff-increase assumption.
- PLF 2026 press report: TND 3,138m proposed for STEG and TND 1,855m for STIR, for TND 4,993m combined; Brent assumption US$63.3/bbl (SRC-TG-166).
- Parliamentary committee report on the 2027 draft budget (SRC-TG-174, PDF pp. 49, 51–52): Brent assumption USD 80/bbl, proposed performance measures TND 600m, and estimated TND 172m extra subsidy for a USD 1/bbl increase. The company split and 2026 comparison remain attributed to the press (SRC-TG-166, SRC-TG-167, SRC-TG-170).

sections.heading: Why confidence is what it is
sections.content: The World Bank supplies a scenario projection from a single financial model (SRC-TG-105). The parliamentary report corroborates the aggregate proposed subsidy and oil-price assumption (SRC-TG-174). Confidence is lower for the company split and prior-year draft figures available through press summaries.

sections.heading: Links to other sectors
sections.content: The finding concerns STEG and energy-sector public finances; no distinct cross-sector effect is established in the sources reviewed.

resolvedSources.title: Tunisia Energy Reliability, Efficiency, and Governance Improvement Program (TEREG) (P507304), Program Appraisal Document, Report No. PADHP00156
resolvedSources.extracts:
Page 2, para. 5:

> Tunisia is facing a deep energy challenge due to its heavy reliance on fossil fuel imports to meet its energy needs, notably natural gas, which constitutes a large part of electricity production. The electricity mix relies primarily on natural gas (94.4 percent). [...] In 2023, Tunisia recorded an energy deficit of 52 percent of its primary energy needs, compared to 20 percent in 2012. Natural gas imports are responsible for close to 40 percent of the energy trade deficit.

English gloss: the electricity mix relies mainly on natural gas (94.4%, no year given). The
energy deficit was 52% of primary needs in 2023, against 20% in 2012. Gas imports cause close
to 40% of the energy trade deficit.

Page 2, para. 6:

> This strategy aims to achieve 35 percent of RE in the energy mix by 2030 with a target of 4,800 MW of RE capacity by 2030 and 8,350 MW by 2035, compared to 516 MW at the end of 2023.

English gloss: the 2022 updated strategy aims for 35% renewables "in the energy mix" by 2030,
4,800 MW of renewable capacity by 2030 and 8,350 MW by 2035, against 516 MW installed at the end
of 2023.

Page 2, para. 7:

> As of mid-2024, STEG accounts for 97 percent of the country's electricity production, with the remainder coming from the private RE sector, including rooftop solar projects. [...] By the end of 2023, Tunisia had an installed generation capacity of 5982 MW. [...] Tunisia's electricity grid is interconnected with Algeria and Libya, and electricity imports increased to cover 12 percent of electricity demand in 2023.

English gloss: in mid-2024 STEG produced 97% of electricity and the rest came from private
renewables. Installed capacity was 5,982 MW at the end of 2023. Electricity imports from the
Algerian and Libyan interconnections covered 12% of demand in 2023.

Page 2, para. 8:

> Despite the Government's efforts, the challenging financial situation of STEG as the main buyer has hindered scaling up private investment in RE.

English gloss: STEG's difficult finances as the main buyer have held back private investment in
renewables.

Page 3, para. 9 b) and c):

> The difference is due to especially high variable cost of electricity generation, estimated at US$0.11 per kWh in 2023, driven by Tunisia's reliance on expensive natural gas for over 95 percent of its power generation, most of which is imported from Algeria.

> Between 2016 and 2022, the peak electricity demand grew by 5.5 percent per year, while investments in new generation capacity were lagging. This has led to an increased risk of electricity shortages during peak hours, estimated at 770 MW (about 16 percent of peak demand).

English gloss: the variable generation cost was about US$0.11/kWh in 2023 because gas, mostly
imported from Algeria, supplies over 95% of generation. Peak demand grew 5.5% a year in
2016-2022 while generation investment lagged. The risk of peak-hour shortage is estimated at
770 MW, about 16% of peak demand.

Page 25, para. 76:

> The reliance on imported natural gas, partially indexed to Brent prices, exposes the country and STEG to cost risks from fluctuations in global energy prices and foreign exchange (FX) rates.

English gloss: imported gas, partly indexed to Brent, exposes Tunisia and STEG to world energy
price and exchange rate risk.

Page 36, DLI 8 verification protocol:

> DLR 8.1: STEG adopts a least-cost 10-year power generation and transmission investment plan consistent with the Tunisian Government's energy transition objectives and is approved by MIME. [...] DLR 8.1 verified for the year 2026 and DLR 8.2 verified for the year 2028

English gloss: a disbursement condition requires STEG to adopt a least-cost 10-year generation and
transmission investment plan, approved by the ministry, to be verified for 2026.

Page 3, para. 9 a) ii (added for FND-TG-221):

> High technical and commercial electricity losses. In 2023, total network losses stood at 18.4 percent, due to commercial losses (mainly fraud), under-spending on operation and maintenance (O&M), aging network assets, and lack of advanced metering infrastructure (AMI).

English gloss: total network losses were 18.4% in 2023, caused by commercial losses (mainly fraud),
under-spending on operation and maintenance, ageing assets, and no advanced metering.

Page 3, para. 9 c) (continued, added for FND-TG-220):

> c) Challenge #3: Deterioration of electricity supply reliability due to tight power generation reserve margin and lagging investments in electricity T&D networks . STEG financial situation has exacerbated implementation of its capacity expansion plan. [...] Furthermore, the financial difficulties of STEG have affected the reliability of the electricity supply and the implementation of the company's distribution investment plan. The impact of major climatic events such as the storm on January 24, 2019, and heavy rainfall in 2021 on the Quality of Service (QoS) is evident in the increased number of transient and permanent interruptions.

English gloss: STEG's financial difficulties have hurt supply reliability and delayed its
distribution investment plan. Storms (January 2019) and heavy rain (2021) increased interruptions.

Footnote 12 (page 20):

> In 2019 alone, storms led to over 5.6 million TND in damages and drove a sharp rise in energy not supplied (ENS) from 6.3 GWh in 2018 to 10 GWh. More recently, a nationwide blackout in 2023 underscored the grid's vulnerability to extreme climatic conditions.

English gloss: energy not supplied rose from 6.3 GWh (2018) to 10 GWh (2019) after storms. A
nationwide blackout occurred in 2023 (no date given).

Page 5, para. 16:

> PDO-Level Outcome Indicator 3 (Custom) / DLI 3: Reduction in the total electricity losses (technical and commercial) (percentage).

Results framework, DLI 3:

> DLR 3: Overall electricity losses (technical and commercial) have been reduced to 15 percent. (Percentage)

English gloss: the programme pays out against cutting total losses to 15%.

Page 2, para. 6 (added for FND-TG-191 and 192):

> Since 2010, the country has promoted energy efficiency and RE, notably through its solar rooftop program for the residential and commercial sectors, enabling the installation of 250 MW to date.

English gloss: the rooftop solar programme (residential and commercial) had installed 250 MW
by the time of writing (document dated April 2025).

Page 2, para. 7 (added for FND-TG-191 and 192):

> The RE capacity installed amounts to 516 MW, out of which 45 percent is owned by STEG and 55 percent by private investors. [...] In 2015, a regulatory framework was established to attract private investors through: (a) the concession regime for large independent power producer (IPP) projects; (b) the authorization regime for medium-size IPPs of up to 10MW for solar and 30MW for wind; and (c) self-generation by industrial firms, including corporate power purchase agreements (PPAs).

English gloss: installed renewable capacity was 516 MW (end 2023), 45% STEG-owned and 55%
private. The 2015 framework has three routes: concessions for large IPPs, authorisations for
IPPs up to 10 MW solar and 30 MW wind, and industrial self-generation including corporate PPAs.

Pages 2-3, para. 8 (added for FND-TG-191 and 192):

> Despite the Government's efforts, the challenging financial situation of STEG as the main buyer has hindered scaling up private investment in RE. [...] The process of developing new RE capacities owned and operated by the private sector has been relatively slow due to learning phase from initial experiences with renewable IPPs, increased costs following the COVID-19 pandemic, and a combination of bureaucratic inefficiencies and financial risks, but encouraging signs suggest that RE development is accelerating [...] In 2019, a 500 MW solar tender was launched of which 200 MW is under construction and 300 MW is nearing financial close. In 2022, a 1,700 MW tender (1,100 MW solar and 600 MW wind) was launched in three rounds, incorporating lessons learned from the 2019 tender. In December 2024, 500 MW of solar capacity was awarded for the first round, with competitive bids ranging from 3.1 to 3.3 USc per kWh, with the remaining capacity to be awarded over the next two years.

English gloss: STEG's weak finances as main buyer have held back private renewable investment.
Private capacity has come slowly because of a learning phase, post-COVID cost increases,
bureaucratic inefficiency and financial risk. Of the 2019 500 MW solar tender, 200 MW was under
construction and 300 MW near financial close (as of April 2025). The 2022 tender (1,100 MW solar,
600 MW wind) awarded 500 MW of solar in December 2024 at 3.1-3.3 US cents/kWh.

Page 24, para. 75 (added for FND-TG-192):

> However, risks exist in implementing the RE plan, which aims to significantly increase RE capacity from 516 MW at the end of 2023 to 3,300 MW by 2028, therefore impacting production costs and STEG's financial viability.

English gloss: the renewable plan aims to go from 516 MW at the end of 2023 to 3,300 MW by 2028;
the World Bank flags implementation risk.

Page 29, results table, DLI 1 (added for FND-TG-220):

> Baseline | Prior Results | Period 1 | Period 2 | Period 3 | Period 4
> 1:DLI1: Improved reliability of electricity supply (Minutes )
> 137 | | 135 | 133 | 130 | 128

Page 38, DLI 1 verification protocol:

> DLR 1: SAIDI is reduced from a baseline value of 137 in 2023 minutes to 128 minutes in 2028.

English gloss: SAIDI (average interruption minutes per customer per year) was 137 minutes in
2023. The programme path is 135, 133, 130 and then 128 minutes by 2028 (period 4 = Dec 2028).

Page 34, DLI 3 data protocol (added for FND-TG-221):

> STEG collects at the end of the year information about total injected power to the grid and amount of electricity sales. Total injected power should consider net generation of STEG's own power plants +imported power through interconnection + IPP's generation-auto consumption. The sales volume corresponds to the quantities of electricity sold plus the quantities recovered from fraud and prorated amounts. Losses in percent are calculated using the formula: [(electricity injected into the grid – volume of electricity sales)/total electricity injected]x100

Page 39, DLI 3 verification protocol:

> Losses in percent are calculated using the formula: [(Energy injected into the grid – volume of electricity sales) / total electricity injected] × 100where total injected power is (net generation of STEG's own power plants +purchased power through interconnection + IPP's generation-auto consumption), electricity sold is the total amount of electricity sales.

English gloss: the World Bank and STEG loss rate is (energy injected minus sales) divided by
energy injected. Energy injected is STEG net generation plus imports plus IPP output (minus
self-consumption). Sales include recovered fraud and pro-rata amounts. ONEM instead divides
network losses by gross production (SRC-TG-222).

Page 26, results framework, DLI 3 (added for FND-TG-221):

> DLI3: Reduction in the total electricity losses (technical and commercial) (Percentage) DLI
> Dec/2023 18.40 | Dec/2028 15

Page 29, results table, DLI 3 path:

> 18.40 | | 17 | 16 | 15.50 | 15

English gloss: the loss baseline is 18.4% (December 2023). The target is 15% by December 2028,
via 17%, 16% and 15.5%.
resolvedSources.notes:
The cover is marked "FOR OFFICIAL USE ONLY", but the document is publicly listed and
downloadable on the World Bank documents site (text version at the URL above, dated 4 April
2025). Page numbers are the "Page n" footers in the text version. The document gives two gas
shares: 94.4% (para. 5, no year) and "over 95 percent" (para. 9). The 35% target "in the energy
mix" by 2030 is attributed to the updated (2022) strategy by this document only. The strategy
synthesis (SRC-TG-103) mentions only the earlier 2016 target of 30% of the electricity mix and
states no 2030 share for the new strategy. IRENA (SRC-TG-106) gives 30%.
Its 8,350 MW for 2035 matches p. 17 of SRC-TG-103, not p. 12.

resolvedSources.title: Tunisia - 2021 Article IV Consultation, Press Release, Staff Report and Statement by the Executive Director (IMF Country Report No. 21/44)
resolvedSources.extracts:
PDF p. 14, staff report, SOE paragraph and footnotes 5-6:

> To meet liquidity needs, SOEs also resort to bank financing (the stock of bank loans to SOEs is about 17 percent of GDP), in particular from state-owned banks (SOBs), and have accumulated arrears. The government itself also has even larger arrears to SOEs (Text Figure 2). This reflects poor financial management and governance of SOEs, a pricing policy that does not cover costs, bloated costs [...]

> 5 Almost 40 percent of transfers are directed to three SOEs in the form of subsidies for cereals, fuel, and electricity.

> 6 At end-June 2020, the stock of SOEs' arrears to the government was estimated at TD 6.2 billion and the stock of government arrears to SOEs at TD 8.8 billion.

PDF p. 20, "Immediate priorities", energy subsidies bullet:

> Energy subsidies. The 2021 budget foresees a decline in energy subsidies to 0.3 percent of GDP, with monthly price changes limited to 2 percent under the automatic fuel price adjustment mechanism. However, oil prices are currently projected to exceed the US$45 per barrel envisaged in the 2021 budget. Staff advised reforming the adjustment mechanism for the three main fuels by letting prices at the pump move more closely with import prices and widening the band for monthly price adjustments. In the context of a broader reform of STEG, the authorities should also consider increasing electricity and gas tariffs, while preserving social tariffs for poor households.

PDF p. 22, section C "Reforming SOEs and Reducing Fiscal Risks", para. 23:

> An immediate audit of arrears and urgent clearance strategy for the largest firms, starting with STIR, STEG, and the Office des Céréales.

PDF p. 75, annex on SOEs, para. 16:

> The major SOEs are suffering structural losses because they operate with regulated pricing policies that do not align with the charges incurred. For companies that remain in the public domain, a reform of subsidized tariffs to progressively allow cost-recovery levels would [...]

English gloss: the 2021 budget assumed energy subsidies would fall to 0.3% of GDP at a US$45
oil price, with monthly fuel price moves capped at 2% under the automatic mechanism; staff advised
widening the band and raising electricity and gas tariffs while keeping social tariffs. At
end-June 2020 the government owed SOEs TD 8.8 billion and SOEs owed the government TD 6.2 billion.
Almost 40% of transfers go to three SOEs as subsidies for cereals, fuel and electricity. Major SOEs
make structural losses because regulated prices do not cover costs.
resolvedSources.notes:
- Text copied from the PDF text layer (PDF saved by WebFetch from the URL above; direct curl is
  blocked by the IMF site). Page numbers are PDF page numbers.
- The arrears figures cover all SOEs, not STEG alone.
- 0.3% of GDP is a 2021 budget projection at a US$45 oil price, not an outturn.

resolvedSources.title: Tunisie: les subventions énergétiques vont baisser de 13% en 2026
resolvedSources.extracts:
Article body (28 October 2025):

> Selon le projet de loi de finances 2026, les aides à l'électricité et aux produits pétroliers devraient passer de 5 719 millions de dinars en 2025 à 4 993 millions, soit une baisse de 13%. Cette réduction permettra au budget de réaliser une économie d'environ 726 millions de dinars.

> Les subventions seront réparties entre la Société tunisienne de l'électricité et du gaz (Steg), qui recevra 3 138 millions de dinars, et la Société tunisienne des industries de raffinage (Stir), qui bénéficiera de 1 855 millions de dinars.

> Le budget repose sur des hypothèses prudentes, notamment un prix moyen du baril de Brent à 63,3 dollars, la stabilité du taux de change et une hausse de la consommation nationale estimée à 6% pour les produits pétroliers et 3% pour l'électricité. Par ailleurs, une partie des dettes accumulées par la Stir et la Steg sur plusieurs années sera régularisée, à hauteur de 670 millions de dinars au total.

> Le taux moyen de subvention pour les produits pétroliers restera de 27%, tandis que les bonbonnes de gaz domestique bénéficieront du taux le plus élevé, à 71%, afin de protéger surtout les familles à revenus faibles et moyens.

English gloss: according to the 2026 draft finance law, electricity and petroleum subsidies fall
from 5,719 MDT in 2025 to 4,993 MDT in 2026 (-13%), with 3,138 MDT for STEG and 1,855 MDT for
STIR. Assumptions: Brent at US$63.3, stable exchange rate, consumption +6% for oil products and
+3% for electricity. 670 MDT of accumulated STIR and STEG debts are to be regularised. Average
subsidy rate on oil products 27%; LPG bottles 71%.
resolvedSources.notes:
- Press report of the PLF 2026 (draft), not the adopted law. Tier C.
- The 5,719 MDT figure for 2025 conflicts with the 7,112 MDT "Carburants" line in the Ministry's
  execution report (SRC-TG-160). The two may differ in scope (for example, whether arrears
  regularisations are included) or in vintage (revised estimate vs appropriation). Not resolved.
- Text extracted from the page HTML.

resolvedSources.title: Budget 2027 : 11,846 milliards de dinars prévus pour les subventions
resolvedSources.extracts:
Article body (22 October 2026):

> Le projet de budget de l'Etat pour l'exercice 2027 prévoit une enveloppe de 11846 millions de de dinars (MD) au titre des dépenses de subvention, selon le document du projet de budget.

> Selon les résultats de l'exécution du budget de l'État à fin août, les dépenses de subvention ont atteint 4496 MD, en hausse de 6 % par rapport à la même période de 2025, soit un taux d'exécution de l'ordre de 46 % par rapport aux prévisions.

> Les dépenses de subvention des hydrocarbures et de l'électricité devraient atteindre environ 7090 MD en 2027, dont 3676 MD pour la Société tunisienne de l'électricité et du gaz (STEG) et 3414 MD pour la Société Tunisienne des Industries de Raffinage (STIR).

> Ces prévisions reposent sur l'hypothèse d'un prix moyen du baril de pétrole Brent de 80 dollars, contre 63,3 dollars dans les hypothèses retenues pour le budget de l'État de 2026.

> Ces estimations prennent également en compte le règlement d'une partie des dettes de la STIR pour les années 2022 et 2024, soit environ 320 MD, ainsi que le règlement d'une partie des dettes de la STEG au titre des exercices allant de 2017 à 2023, soit environ 500 MD.

> La part de la subvention dans le coût réel est estimée à 15 % pour l'essence, 18 % pour l'électricité à haute et moyenne tension, 22 % pour le gasoil 50, 23 % pour le gasoil normal, 41 % pour le gaz haute et moyenne pression, 44 % pour l'électricité à basse tension destinée aux ménages et 60 % pour le gaz à basse pression destiné aux ménages, outre 75 % pour les bouteilles de gaz à usage domestique.

English gloss: the 2027 draft budget plans 11,846 MDT of subsidies. Hydrocarbon and electricity
subsidies are about 7,090 MDT in 2027 (3,676 STEG, 3,414 STIR), assuming Brent at US$80 against
US$63.3 in the 2026 budget. This includes settling about 500 MDT of STEG arrears for 2017-2023 and
320 MDT of STIR arrears. Subsidy as a share of real cost: 44% for household low-voltage
electricity, 60% for household low-pressure gas, 18% for high/medium-voltage electricity, 15% for
gasoline, 75% for LPG bottles.

resolvedSources.title: فاتورة الدعم في تونس المحروقات في الصدارة وضغوط متزايدة على الميزانية (The subsidy bill in Tunisia, hydrocarbons first and growing pressure on the budget)
resolvedSources.extracts:
Article body (31 October 2026), citing the draft 2027 state budget and the 2027-2029
medium-term budget framework:

> تتجه نفقات الدعم في تونس إلى تسجيل ارتفاع ملحوظ خلال سنة 2027، وفق تقديرات مشروع ميزانية الدولة، لتبلغ نحو 11 مليارًا و846 مليون دينار، مقابل 9 مليارات و772 مليون دينار مرسمة بقانون المالية لسنة 2026، أي بزيادة تناهز 2 مليار و74 مليون دينار، وبنسبة 21.2 بالمائة.

English gloss: subsidy spending is set to rise markedly in 2027 per the draft state budget, to
about 11,846 MDT against 9,772 MDT in the 2026 finance law, an increase of about 2,074 MDT (21.2%).

> وتربط وثيقة مشروع ميزانية الدولة الزيادة المسجلة في نفقات دعم المحروقات خلال سنة 2026، أساسًا، بارتفاع أسعار النفط في الأسواق العالمية. فقد بلغ معدل سعر برميل النفط من نوع «برنت» إلى موفى أوت 2026 نحو 91.21 دولارًا، مقابل 71.21 دولارًا خلال الفترة نفسها من سنة 2025.

English gloss: the draft budget attributes the 2026 rise in hydrocarbon subsidy spending mainly
to world oil prices; Brent averaged about US$91.21 to end-August 2026 against US$71.21 a year
earlier.

> كما أشار المشروع إلى أن معدل سعر النفط المتوقع لكامل سنة 2026 يناهز 90 دولارًا للبرميل، في حين لم تتجاوز الفرضية المعتمدة عند إعداد قانون المالية لسنة 2026 نحو 63.3 دولارًا.

English gloss: the draft expects an average of about US$90 per barrel for 2026, while the 2026
finance law assumed about US$63.3.

> فوفق تقديرات وزارة المالية، فإن ارتفاع سعر برميل النفط بدولار واحد يؤدي إلى زيادة نفقات الدعم بنحو 172 مليون دينار، في حين تؤدي زيادة سعر صرف الدولار بعشرة مليمات إلى ارتفاع هذه النفقات بنحو 59 مليون دينار.

English gloss: per Ministry of Finance estimates, each US$1 rise in the oil price raises subsidy
spending by about 172 MDT; a 10-millime rise in the dollar exchange rate adds about 59 MDT.

> تقدر حاجيات التمويل الضرورية لتوازن منظومة المحروقات والكهرباء والغاز خلال سنة 2027 بنحو 6 مليارات و870 مليون دينار. غير أن منحة الدولة المبرمجة بعنوان دعم المحروقات تبلغ 7 مليارات و90 مليون دينار، بعد الأخذ في الاعتبار تسوية جزء من المتخلدات واتخاذ إجراءات لتحسين الأداء المالي والتجاري للمؤسسات المعنية.

English gloss: the financing need to balance the hydrocarbons, electricity and gas system in 2027
is about 6,870 MDT, but the programmed state grant is 7,090 MDT after including settlement of part
of the arrears and performance measures.

> وفي المقابل، يتضمن المشروع إجراءات يُنتظر أن توفر 600 مليون دينار، من خلال تحسين الأداء المالي والتجاري للشركة التونسية للكهرباء والغاز، وتقليص الخسائر على شبكة الكهرباء، والتحكم في كلفة الإنتاج، إلى جانب مراقبة مسالك توزيع الغاز المسال الموجه للاستهلاك المنزلي.

English gloss: the draft includes measures expected to save 600 MDT by improving STEG's financial
and commercial performance, reducing electricity network losses, controlling production cost and
monitoring the distribution of household LPG.

> كما يوضح التقرير أن الضمانات الممنوحة خلال سنة 2025 لقطاعي الطاقة والصناعة بلغت 2.4068 مليار دينار، أي ما يعادل 45.7 بالمائة من إجمالي ضمانات الدولة الممنوحة للمؤسسات العمومية خلال تلك السنة، ومن بينها 974.1 مليون دينار لفائدة الشركة التونسية للكهرباء والغاز و400 مليون دينار لفائدة الشركة التونسية لصناعات التكرير.

English gloss: according to the report on transfers and guarantees, state guarantees granted in
2025 to the energy and industry sectors were 2.4068 billion dinars (45.7% of all state guarantees
to public enterprises), including 974.1 MDT for STEG and 400 MDT for STIR.
resolvedSources.notes:
- Press summary of official budget documents (PLF 2027, medium-term budget framework, report on
  transfers and guarantees). Tier C until the official documents are opened.
- The per-dollar sensitivity (172 MDT) differs from the 140-150 MDT quoted by an expert in
  SRC-TG-168.
- Text extracted from the page HTML.

resolvedSources.title: Report on the draft economic balance and state budget for 2027
resolvedSources.publisher: Assemblée des représentants du peuple, Tunisia
resolvedSources.extracts:
PDF pp. 51–52, proposed subsidy expenditure. Short extracts transcribed from the Arabic text:

> تم تخصيص مبلغ 11846 م.د لنفقات الدعم

> وتخصيص 7090 م.د

English gloss: the proposal allocates 11,846 million TND to subsidies in total, including a 7,090 million TND hydrocarbon subsidy appropriation shared between STIR and STEG. The cited passage gives no allocation by utility. These are budget proposals, not cash payments.

PDF p. 51, oil-price assumption: Brent at USD 80/bbl. PDF p. 52, sensitivity estimates: 172 million TND per USD 1/bbl increase and 59 million TND per 10-millime increase in the dollar exchange rate. The document also describes 600 million TND of proposed STEG performance measures and approximately 820 million TND in combined arrears settlement for STIR and STEG. The combined arrears figure is not specific to STEG.
